cards.explanation: The answer is so the king won't suffer loss. The text says the satraps are accountable to the three administrators “…so that the king would not suffer loss.” Darius, the king over this kingdom, wants somebody keeping an eye on things. With 120 satraps out there, I'd want a few supervisors too. Daniel is one of them.

The answer is kingdom. The king plans to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. That's every satrap, every administrator and everybody else. I can barely supervise one batch, and the king plans to hand Daniel the entire operation.

The answer is False. They found nothing. The text says they could find no charge or corruption, and that no negligence or corruption was found in him. These men were looking hard and still had nothing to show for it, friends. When you can't find a single crumb on a man's record, that says a lot about him.

The answer is trustworthy. That's the reason the text gives for why the officials came up empty. Verse 4 says they found no charge “…because he was trustworthy…” and no negligence or corruption was found in him. That's a hard record to dig through, friends.

The answer is the law of his God. The men tell each other, “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.” They know his work is spotless, friends. So the one place left to attack is his faith.

The answer is King Darius. The decree says anyone who petitions any god or man “…except you, O king…” will be thrown into the lions' den. The men are talking to Darius, so the one exception is Darius himself. Thirty days of everybody asking the king and only the king. I think that decree has someone's pride all over it.

The answer is True. The men tell Darius to sign the document “…so that it cannot be changed…” and they say that's in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed. Once the ink dries, it's done, friends. They had that part planned out carefully.

The answer is that Daniel prays just as he had done before. He goes into his house, and three times a day he gets down on his knees, prays and gives thanks to his God, “…just as he had done before.” The decree didn't change his routine one bit. Some people change plans when the rules do. Daniel isn't one of them.

The answer is Jerusalem. His upper room windows open toward Jerusalem, and that's where he kneels, prays and gives thanks. Daniel was one of the exiles from Judah (Daniel 6:13), so I think that direction means something to him. That's my guess, friends, not the text's.

The answer is distressed. That's the word the text uses. When the king hears what the men say, Darius is deeply distressed and sets his mind on delivering Daniel. Whatever the men expected, the king doesn't look pleased with how this is turning out.

The answer is True. The text says the king set his mind on delivering Daniel and labored until sundown to rescue him. That's real effort from a king, friends. Darius isn't just sitting on the throne watching.

The answer is that the king says God should deliver him. Right as Daniel is thrown in, Darius tells him, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” I think that's a king with no more moves left, but that's my guess. Notice he says it about Daniel's God.

The answer is changed. The king seals the stone with his own signet ring and the rings of his nobles, “…so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.” It's a lot of rings for one stone, friends. Those rings were there to keep everything exactly as it was.

The answer is whether Daniel's God was able to deliver him. In a voice of anguish, the king cries, “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” He calls Daniel a servant of the living God. After a night with no sleep, that's the question he has.

The answer is angel. Daniel says, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” Daniel doesn't talk about his own courage, friends. He gives the credit to God and the angel He sent. That's a pretty humble report from a man who just spent a night in a lions' den.

The answer is that he was found innocent in God's sight. That's the reason Daniel gives when he says the lions have not hurt him: “…for I was found innocent in His sight…” He adds that he has done no wrong against the king, too.

The answer is that he had trusted in his God. When Daniel is lifted out, no wounds whatsoever are found on him, “…because he had trusted in his God.” That's the reason the text gives, friends. It's the same kind of trust Daniel showed when he kept praying as he always had.

The answer is False. Darius writes, “…He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end.” So the king says God's kingdom will not come to an end. It's a big statement, friends, from a man whose own decrees got stuck.

The answer is in the heavens and on the earth. Darius writes that God “…performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions.” The king's letter reaches every nation and language. He's telling the whole kingdom what happened.
